newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zaire rebels accused of "final solution" on Hutus.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels accused of "final solution" on Hutus.

text.p: U.N. agencies on Friday accused Zaire's mainly Tutsi rebels of trying to achieve a "final solution" by condemning thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees to a slow and cruel death.
Aid agencies expressed outrage at rebel treatment of the refugees following reports that 30,000 Hutus had fled rebel-held territory soon after the exodus of 55,000 others earlier this week.

"Eighty thousand people are condemned to a slow and cruel death. The expression 'final solution' is not exaggerated," said Christiane Berthiaume, spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP), in a reference to the notorious Nazi extermination policy against Jews in World War Two.
"They (the rebels) want these people to die. There's food over there but these people are starving. If the refugees go into the jungle, they will die. We are powerless."

The Rwandans are the rump of two million Hutus who fled in 1994 in fear of reprisal for the Hutu-led genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates. They are widely considered as killers by many Tutsi survivors in their overcrowded homeland.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR urged governments to put pressure on the rebels ahead of a Monday briefing to the U.N. Security Council by its UNHCR chief, Sadako Ogata.

"We're deeply concerned by a series of reports of violence against the refugees and against local people," spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said. "We are asking the (rebel) alliance to answer questions about the fate of these refugees."
Apart from Rwanda and Uganda, which back the rebels, diplomats say the governments of the United States and Britain have varying degrees of influence on rebel leader Laurent Kabila.

"I don't know exactly how much influence the United States may or may not have on Kabila but obviously somebody's going to be able to influence him. He obviously has some friends out there," O'Toole said.
UNHCR has received reports suggesting that the camp of Biaro, 45 km (25 miles) south of the rebel-held eastern city of Kisangani, is empty of its 30,000 refugees, O'Toole said.
Agencies have been denied access there but an aid worker trapped in Biaro on Tuesday reported the arrival of a train full of rebels, followed by looting and fighting, O'Toole said.
The aid worker reported the Hutus left Biaro soon afterwards and headed south in an orderly manner. O'Toole said other reports said the rebels were moving the Hutus south.
Aid workers on Thursday found nearby Kasese camp empty of 55,000 refugees after the rebels sealed the area off on Monday.
O'Toole said Kasese had been stripped bare. Huge water tanks had disappeared and equipment and medicine had been looted.

"The situation is completely unacceptable," O'Toole said. "We can't go on providing aid for refugees, trying to locate refugees, chasing them from one place to another to help them, only to find a series of obstacles blocking our way."
